rubric.why: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through leaf stomata.
rubric.description: Defines transpiration as the loss of water vapour from the plant, especially its aerial parts or leaves.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining transpiration as water-vapour loss from the plant.

rubric.why: Light promotes stomatal opening, while higher temperature increases evaporation; both generally raise the rate of transpiration.
rubric.description: Explains the effects of light and temperature on transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that greater light intensity opens stomata and increases transpiration, and 1 mark for stating that higher temperature increases evaporation and transpiration.

rubric.why: Humidity affects the water-vapour gradient between the leaf and the surrounding air.
rubric.description: States that high humidity decreases transpiration, or that dry air increases it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct effect of humidity.

rubric.why: Wind carries moist air away from the leaf, while water availability affects stomatal opening and water loss.
rubric.description: Describes the effect of wind or soil-water availability on transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing either the effect of wind or the effect of water availability.

modelAnswer: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata of leaves.
Light: greater light intensity usually opens stomata and increases the rate of transpiration.
Temperature: higher temperature increases evaporation and usually increases transpiration.
Humidity: high humidity decreases transpiration, while dry air increases it.
Wind: moving air carries moist air away from the leaf and usually increases transpiration.
Soil water: adequate water supports transpiration, while water shortage causes stomata to close and reduces the rate.
